Phase-contrast imaging

Words: 46
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Phase-contrast imaging converts spatial phase changes of light into intensity differences by interference with a reference field. In an off-resonant atomic cloud, the optical phase carries information about column density. Weak probing can support repeated measurements with reduced absorption, although destructiveness still depends on detuning and probe strength.

Huygens-Fresnel principle

Words: 162 Articles: 2
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
The Huygens-Fresnel principle describes propagation by coherent addition of secondary-wave contributions from a wavefront or aperture. Their complex amplitudes, including relative wave phases, must be summed before calculating light intensity. The Fresnel propagator follows by retaining quadratic propagation wave phase in the paraxial approximation.

Huygens' principle

Words: 34
Huygens-Fresnel principle OurBigBook.com
Each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, whose envelope gives the next wavefront. The geometric construction gives refraction from secondary wavelets. The Huygens-Fresnel principle additionally keeps the amplitudes and phases needed to calculate interference and diffraction.

Refraction from secondary wavelets

Words: 94
Huygens-Fresnel principle OurBigBook.com
Let a plane incident wavefront first meet a flat interface at A, and let another point B on that front reach C on the interface after Δt. Its path has length BC=v1​Δt. The secondary wavelet from A has radius AD=v2​Δt in the second medium; the new wavefront through C is tangent to it at D. Right triangles with common hypotenuse AC give sinθ1​=BC/AC and sinθ2​=AD/AC, where both ray angles are measured from the interface normal. Consequently sinθ1​/sinθ2​=v1​/v2​=n2​/n1​, which is Snell's law. The construction uses phase velocities in homogeneous isotropic media.

Scalar diffraction theory

Words: 118 Articles: 1
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Scalar diffraction theory approximates light by one complex field satisfying a scalar wave equation. Aperture propagation is represented by an integral of secondary contributions, with vector polarization of waves and detailed electromagnetic edge conditions suppressed. The approximation is useful for many apertures large compared with wavelength, but is not an exact substitute for Maxwell equations at arbitrary apertures.

Babinet's principle

Words: 71
Scalar diffraction theory OurBigBook.com
In linear scalar diffraction theory, complementary aperture transmissions t and 1−t give complex fields Ut​+U1−t​=U0​, where U0​ is the unobstructed field under identical illumination. Away from the direct beam in Fraunhofer diffraction, their diffracted fields differ by a sign and have equal intensity. Intensities do not generally add: in particular, complementary on-axis Fresnel diffraction patterns need not have equal intensity. The ideal scalar statement does not incorporate vector boundary details at a real conducting edge.

Spectral phase

Words: 9
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
The wave phase of a complex Fourier transform as a function of frequency.

Interferometer

Words: 575 Articles: 11
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
An interferometer combines waves from two or more paths to measure their interference.

Rayleigh interferometer

Words: 57
Interferometer OurBigBook.com
A Rayleigh interferometer compares optical paths through a sample and a reference. A path-length difference Δℓ shifts the interference phase by 2πΔℓ/λ. In analytical ultracentrifugation, sample and reference sectors produce concentration-dependent fringe shifts, allowing radial concentration scans without requiring the solute to absorb at the probe wavelength.[ref]

Division of wavefront

Words: 28
Interferometer OurBigBook.com
In division of wavefront, different spatial portions of an incident wavefront are selected and propagated so that their fields overlap. Double-slit interference is an example. The selected portions need sufficient spatial optical coherence for stable interference fringes.

Division of amplitude

Words: 34
Interferometer OurBigBook.com
In division of amplitude, a partially reflecting interface sends parts of the same incident wavefront into separate paths that are later recombined. A Michelson interferometer is an example. The resulting interference visibility depends on relative optical path length, polarization of waves, intensity balance and optical coherence.

Interferogram

Words: 53
Interferometer OurBigBook.com
An interferogram records detected light intensity produced by interference as a controlled position, phase or delay is varied. In Fourier transform spectroscopy, the variable is the delay between two copies of the same field. Removing the constant background gives a correlation signal whose Fourier transform determines the source's spectral power density, subject to the measured delay window and instrumental response.

Astronomical interferometer

Words: 392 Articles: 6
Interferometer OurBigBook.com
An astronomical interferometer combines observations from separated collecting locations to infer angular source structure. Its projected interferometric baseline determines the angular spatial frequency sampled. Amplitude and intensity interferometers measure different coherence observables; a Michelson stellar interferometer combines optical field amplitudes.

Two-element radio interferometer (I(θ)=2I0​[1+cos(2πbsinθ/λ+δ)])

Words: 72
Astronomical interferometer OurBigBook.com
A two-element radio interferometer coherently combines signals from two receiving antennas. With equal single-arm wave intensity I0​, projected baseline b, free-space wavelength λ and imposed phase difference δ, its directional response is the displayed formula. It follows by adding the two complex amplitudes and taking the squared modulus. Near the normal to the baseline, the first null is λ/(2b) from a maximum. This narrow response repeats in interference fringes, so a long baseline alone does not give an unambiguous image.

Closure phase (Φ=ϕ12​+ϕ23​+ϕ31​)

Words: 39
Astronomical interferometer OurBigBook.com
For three collectors whose measured pair phases are ϕij​=ϕijsource​+ϵi​−ϵj​, the oriented sum around the triangle cancels the collector-based errors. closure phase retains source phase information, including asymmetry, but does not cancel arbitrary baseline-dependent errors or fill missing spatial-frequency coverage.

Michelson stellar interferometer

Words: 248 Articles: 3
Astronomical interferometer OurBigBook.com
The Michelson stellar interferometer, associated with Albert Abraham Michelson, uses separated collectors and beam-redirection optics to produce interference fringes. The collector spacing determines sensitivity to a stellar angular diameter, independently of the final beam spacing at the combiner. The first null for a uniform disk is D=1.21967λ/α, where α is the full angular diameter. Different surface-brightness laws, including limb darkening, change the null.
Equal-brightness binary-star visibility (g(Y)=g⋆​(Y)cos(πβY/λ))
Words: 191 Articles: 2
Michelson stellar interferometer OurBigBook.com
Let identical spatially incoherent stellar brightness profiles of equal integrated flux be displaced by projected angles ±β/2 along an interferometer baseline. The Fourier shift property makes their normalized signed coherence g(Y)=g⋆​(Y)cos(πβY/λ). The observed visibility is its absolute value. The slow single-star envelope depends on each star's brightness profile, while the oscillatory factor records projected separation. Unequal flux prevents complete cancellation at the binary minima.
Binary separation from visibility-zero spacing (ΔY=λ/β)
Words: 65
Equal-brightness binary-star visibility OurBigBook.com
For two identical equally bright stars, zeros of the binary factor occur at Yj​=(j+1/2)λ/β, where β is separation projected along the baseline. Their repeated spacing is ΔY=λ/β. Multiple samples separate these rapid zeros from zeros of a resolved stellar envelope. Baseline rotation is needed to recover an unknown two-dimensional separation direction; the first zero alone does not determine both diameter and separation.
Uniform-disc binary-star visibility (V(Y)=​x2J1​(x)​cos(πβY/λ)​)
Words: 62
Equal-brightness binary-star visibility OurBigBook.com
Two identical uniform circular discs of angular diameter α and equal flux have g⋆​(Y)=2J1​(x)/x, x=παY/λ, with limiting value one at Y=0. Multiplication by cos(πβY/λ) gives their signed binary coherence. Its first single-disc envelope zero is Y=1.21967λ/α, while the binary modulation has a separate scale λ/β. Limb darkening and other nonuniform profiles change the envelope, not the elementary Fourier shift factor.

Fresnel diffraction

Words: 2k Articles: 20
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Fresnel diffraction describes diffraction when the quadratic propagation wave phase across an aperture must be retained. Its Fresnel propagator becomes the Fraunhofer diffraction description when that curvature is negligible.
A Fresnel diffraction pattern is a map of how propagation changes the wave interference of light from an aperture. It can resemble the opening, develop bright and dark structure near its edges, and eventually approach a Fraunhofer diffraction pattern. The controlling comparison involves wavelength, opening size and propagation distance together; a distance large compared with the opening need not give the far field.
For a monochromatic wave, use time dependence e−iωt, wavenumber k=2π/λ and complex amplitude U. Let U0​(ξ,η) be the transmitted field immediately behind an aperture in the plane z=0. In a homogeneous medium, the scalar paraxial approximation gives
U(x,y,z)≃iλzeikz​∬R2​U0​(ξ,η)exp[λziπ​((x−ξ)2+(y−η)2)]dξdη,z>0.
(1)
This is the two-transverse-coordinate Fresnel propagator, with its carrier eikz restored. It adds complex amplitudes before taking their squared complex modulus to obtain light intensity. It is a scalar paraxial approximation, rather than a full vector solution of Maxwell equations.[ref]
The source in this constructed geometry supplies a plane wave; the observation screen is a plane perpendicular to the optical axis. The right panel isolates the aperture-dependent wave phase that distinguishes Fresnel diffraction from Fraunhofer diffraction. Its vertical scale is in radians, and the drawing's lengths are schematic.
Keeping this wave phase is useful when transporting a field between nearby optical components: both the shape and the complex amplitude matter for subsequent wave interference. A particularly striking feature is that propagation can create a dark centre even from a uniformly illuminated symmetric aperture; the incident wave amplitudes need not be unequal for their outgoing contributions to cancel.

Cornu chord power normalization (P/Popen​=∣F(w+​)−F(w−​)∣2/2)

Words: 208 Articles: 3
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
For normalized Fresnel integrals F(w)=C(w)+iS(w), an interval aperture contributes the chord between its two limiting points on the Cornu spiral. The full unobstructed field is F(+∞)−F(−∞)=1+i, so its squared magnitude is2. Comparing to only the half-plane limit instead of this full chord introduces a factor-of-four normalization error. The formula compares power at one observation point under the same illumination and propagation factors.

Largest contiguous Fresnel aperture (w∗​≃1.20938)

Words: 145 Articles: 2
Cornu chord power normalization OurBigBook.com
The largest radius of the normalized Cornu spiral occurs on its first outer turn at w∗​≃1.20938, where Re[F(w)∗F′(w)]=0. Oddness makes the chord from F(−w∗​) to F(w∗​) attain twice that radius, while the triangle inequality bounds every other chord by the same length. The interval is therefore the strongest freely selectable connected aperture at that observation point, with normalized point power about1.80142. Signed physical limits follow from x=wλz/2​. Existing openings can constrain this optimization.
Pointwise Fresnel gain versus integrated transmitted power
Largest contiguous Fresnel aperture OurBigBook.com
Existing-opening constraint in Fresnel aperture optimization
Words: 70
Largest contiguous Fresnel aperture OurBigBook.com
If a screen already has an interval hole, additional removal cannot reduce that hole. A connected final aperture must contain it, imposing lower/upper endpoint constraints on its Cornu spiral chord. The unrestricted longest chord need not be feasible. For an existing interval 0≤w≤1.76777, constrained chord maximization gives approximately w−​=−1.21578, w+​=2.34054, with point-power ratio1.60257. The two aperture endpoints, rather than just a nominal Fresnel-zone width, determine the received field.

Knife-edge diffraction (T(v)={[1/2−C(v)]2+[1/2−S(v)]2}/2)

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
For an opaque half-plane whose edge lies height h above the direct source–receiver ray, the paraxial parameter is v=h2(d1​+d2​)/(λd1​d2​)​. The unobstructed half-aperture supplies the Cornu spiral chord from v to infinity. Division by the full-aperture chord gives the displayed intensity transmission. It is 1/4 at grazing incidence, approaches one well into the illuminated region and tends to zero deep in shadow.[ref]

Geometric spreading in a moving-receiver diffraction measurement (I(d)∝T[v(d)]/(d1​+d)2)

Words: 53
Knife-edge diffraction OurBigBook.com
A diffraction-loss ratio is normalized to the unobstructed intensity at the same receiver position. With a point source that unobstructed intensity changes as inverse source–receiver distance squared. Moving the receiver can therefore decrease the transmission ratio while increasing its absolute received intensity. The two curves require separate normalization; a Cornu-chord plot alone omits geometric spreading.

Fresnel-Kirchhoff diffraction integral

Words: 71
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
A scalar aperture approximation that sums the secondary waves reaching an observation point. For a point source with incident spherical amplitude Aeiks/s, one common forward-normal convention is
U(P)=iλA​∫A​srK(Q)eik(s+r)​dS.
(2)
Here s and r are source-to-aperture and aperture-to-observer distances and K is an obliquity factor. The Fresnel diffraction approximation retains quadratic path phase; Fraunhofer diffraction additionally neglects the quadratic phase across the aperture. Kirchhoff boundary assumptions do not give an exact electromagnetic solution at a sharp edge.

Zone plate

Words: 215 Articles: 2
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
A concentric diffractive focusing element with successive zone boundaries chosen to differ by half a wavelength of optical path to a focus. Alternating transmitting and absorbing zones suppress cancellation between neighboring half-period zones. For an incident plane wave, the paraxial boundaries satisfy rj2​=jλf. The outermost zone width controls the finest transverse scale, and the focal length varies with wavelength.

Exact half-period zone radii (rn2​=nfλ+n2λ2/4)

Words: 77
Zone plate OurBigBook.com
For a plane wave incident on a flat zone plate, the path difference from radius rn​ to axial focal distance f is f2+rn2​​−f. Setting it equal to nλ/2 gives the title relation. The paraxial limit is rn​≃nfλ​, and the fine outer-zone width is approximately fλ/(2rn​). Alternately removing half-period annuli makes the remaining contributions reinforce at the principal focus. Choosing the number of zones sets the aperture and fabrication scale, not the principal focal distance independently of these radii.

Axial intensity gain of an amplitude zone plate (If​/I0​≃4No2​)

Words: 81
Zone plate OurBigBook.com
For uniform coherent plane-wave illumination, an ideal binary amplitude zone plate transmits alternate Fresnel half-period zones. If No​ complete odd zones are open, every one contributes approximately twice the unobstructed axial complex amplitude, in the same phase, and If​/I0​≃4No2​. This is a local light intensity gain relative to removing the plate and outer stop. It differs from comparison with a finite clear aperture: an aperture containing an odd integer number of half-period zones has axial intensity 4I0​, giving plate-to-aperture ratio No2​. Neither gain is a total power efficiency.

Half-plane shadow-boundary intensity

Words: 67
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
At the geometric shadow boundary of a straight opaque half-plane, the transmitted Fresnel integral is exactly half the unobstructed complex amplitude for ideal point illumination. The Cornu spiral chord is from its origin to one limiting endpoint, rather than between both limiting endpoints. Therefore U/U0​=1/2 and I/I0​=1/4. Half the unobstructed intensity would confuse a field fraction with its square. Edge thickness, source extent and alignment can modify the ideal result.

Arago spot

Words: 56
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
The Arago spot is the bright axial point in the shadow of a circular obstruction under suitably coherent illumination. In ideal scalar diffraction theory, secondary fields from the circular edge arrive in phase on axis. Fresnel diffraction by an opaque disk gives an axial intensity equal to the unobstructed intensity in its paraxial model; this is not a claim that the whole geometric shadow is bright.

Fresnel diffraction by an opaque disk

Words: 64
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
Under the same scalar paraxial assumptions as Fresnel diffraction by a circular aperture, Babinet's principle gives the complementary opaque-disk field Ud​/U0​=eiπNF​ on axis. Its axial intensity equals the unobstructed intensity, producing the Arago spot inside the geometric shadow. The off-axis pattern depends on the full Fresnel integral; it is not obtained by subtracting aperture intensities from the incident intensity. Finite source size, misalignment and imperfect circular edges reduce the ideal spot contrast.

Fresnel diffraction by a circular aperture

Words: 93
Fresnel diffraction OurBigBook.com
For a circular aperture of radius a, paraxial plane-wave illumination and propagation distance z, define NF​=a2/(λz). On axis, the radial Fresnel diffraction integral normalized by the unobstructed field gives
U0​Ua​​=1−eiπNF​,I0​Ia​​=4sin2(2πNF​​).
(3)
For a finite axial point source a distance s before the aperture and detector a distance r after it, replace z by sr/(s+r) in the phase. The formula assumes illumination amplitudes and obliquity factors approximately constant across the aperture. Odd and even numbers of Fresnel half-period zones give bright and dark axial extrema; large local intensity is compatible with global conservation of energy.

Fresnel half-period zone

Phase conjugation creates a returning monochromatic wave whose spatial complex amplitude is proportional to the complex conjugate of the incident field. Fix the time convention throughout:
E(r,t)=Re{U(r)e−iωt},U(r)=A(r)eiϕ(r),Uc​(r)=γA(r)e−iϕ(r).
(18)
Here E is one scalar component of the electric field, A≥0 is the wave amplitude, ω>0 is the angular frequency, and γ is a spatially constant complex number setting the return strength and reference wave phase. The complex conjugation acts on U, including its spatial carrier, while the time factor remains e−iωt. Conjugating both factors would merely give another representation of the same real field. With γ=1, the new real field equals E(r,−t) in this ideal monochromatic wave model; that identity does not assert reversal of an arbitrary pulse or of the apparatus producing it.
The spatial wave phase becomes −ϕ+argγ, so the local wavevector changes from ∇ϕ to −∇ϕ. For example, U=Aei(kx​x+kz​z) with kz​>0 becomes γAe−i(kx​x+kz​z): both components of the wavevector reverse. In a transparent stationary medium with isotropy and positive refractive index, light rays follow the wavevector, giving counterpropagation. The same wavefronts now have opposite propagation normals. This is why phase conjugation can return a distorted beam toward its origin: it reverses the detailed spatial wave phase, rather than requiring that wave phase to be flat.
The attractive application is correction of optical aberrations accumulated on an outward trip. The return uses the distortion itself as the prescription for correction, as the original thin phase-plate cancellation by phase conjugation example makes explicit. An experimentally accessible implementation measures the spatial wave phase and uses a spatial light modulator to generate its negative; digital optical phase conjugation describes an inspected 2010 demonstration of recovery through multiple scattering.

Phase-conjugate mirror (Ureturn​(x,y)=γUincident​(x,y)∗)

A phase-conjugate mirror is an optical device that implements phase conjugation at its return surface. It may generate the return using an independently supplied beam, as in digital optical phase conjugation; its name specifies the field transformation, rather than a particular reflecting material. Conjugating the transverse complex amplitude and launching the returning longitudinal carrier produces the complete reversed wavevector. A spatially constant γ leaves the shape of the wavefront unchanged; a spatially varying γ would add its own wavefront error.
An ordinary flat mirror obeys the law of reflection. At a surface z=L, its reflected plane wave has wavevector (kx​,ky​,−kz​), whereas a phase-conjugate mirror returns (−kx​,−ky​,−kz​). Ordinary specular reflection preserves the tangential wavevector. At normal incidence a single plane wave can therefore look identical in the two cases, apart from an overall wave phase and strength; oblique incidence or a curved wavefront reveals the distinction. In boundary-envelope notation an ideal ordinary mirror multiplies the incident complex amplitude by a constant reflection factor r, while an ideal phase-conjugate mirror returns its complex conjugate times γ.

Digital optical phase conjugation

Phase conjugation OurBigBook.com
Digital optical phase conjugation uses a wavefront sensor and a spatial light modulator to measure an incident field and launch a beam with the opposite spatial wave phase. A phase-only spatial light modulator illuminated uniformly generally does not reproduce the incident wave amplitude as well; exact γU∗ requires the appropriate wave amplitude and polarization of an electromagnetic wave too. The experimentally useful question is how much of the original optical mode can be recovered with the measured and controlled field components.
In 2010, Meng Cui and Changhuei Yang demonstrated digital optical phase conjugation through a prepared multiple scattering sample. They dried mixed-size polystyrene microspheres on cover glass, added immersion oil, and sealed them with another cover glass. A 532 nm laser supplied signal and reference beams. The signal crossed the sample between two objectives; the reference interfered with it on a charge-coupled device. Phase-stepped wave interference recovered the spatial wave phase; a calibrated spatial light modulator imposed its negative on the reference-derived return beam. The reference supplied playback power, without nonlinear mixing pumps. An optical camera read out the recovered signal. With the same sample and a zero-phase spatial light modulator control, the return instead produced a scattering of light pattern. This comparison supports mode recovery by spatial wave phase control, not merely increased illumination. A separate ordinary-mirror control tested source displacements. Finite sampling and collection limited recovery; the system controlled wave phase rather than the complete vector field. These restrictions distinguish demonstrated reconstruction from exact reversal of every scattered component.[ref]

A wavefront connects points with the same wave phase at one specified time. It is a surface, rather than the trajectory of a particular piece of light. For a scalar monochromatic wave written as u(r,t)=A(r)cosΦ(r,t), a wavefront is a connected level set of the phase function Φ; different surfaces can share the same wave phase modulo 2π. A plane wave has planar wavefronts. An outward wave from an ideal point source in a uniform medium has spheres as wavefronts, while an optical lens can turn nearly planar wavefronts into converging ones. The wavefront describes wave phase, not wave amplitude: drawing it does not say how bright the beam is. [ref]

A forward light ray has unit tangent vector dr/ds=∇S/n, so it follows this normal under the stated assumptions. Along that light ray, dS/ds=∇S⋅(dr/ds)=n: the change in S is the optical path length. Its stipulated refractive indices are n1​=1 and n2​=3/2, and its incident angle is 30∘ to the interface normal. At a stationary interface, the frequency and tangential wavevector agree on the two sides: Snell's law gives sinθ2​=1/3, hence θ2​≈19.4712∘. The wavefronts turn while their normal spacing decreases from λ0​ to 2λ0​/3, where λ0​ is the vacuum wavelength. More explicitly, with x normal to the interface and y tangential, take S1​=3​x/2+y/2 for x<0 and S2​=2​x+y/2 for x>0. These functions agree at x=0; the drawn wavefronts are Sj​=mλ0​ at t=0 with ϕ0​=0. This is an exact piecewise plane wave phase construction for the stipulated transparent media, not measured material data. [ref]
The normal-to-wavefront rule requires its assumptions. In a medium with anisotropy, the wavevector remains normal to a smooth wavefront, but the group velocity and energy flux need not follow it. [ref] Near a wave caustic, where multiple light rays meet, one smooth phase function may no longer describe the field; diffraction and the full wave amplitude matter. A wavefront is also not generally a surface of equal pulse arrival time. In a medium with optical dispersion, a monochromatic wave phase moves with the phase velocity, while a sufficiently narrow wave packet follows the group velocity. Even identical optical path lengths at one frequency can give different group delays. The usual equal-travel-time picture needs a common launch reference and a nondispersive ray model; an arbitrary broadband disturbance has no single monochromatic wavefront.[ref]

Optical path length (∫nds)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Wavefront OurBigBook.com
An optical path length measures how much propagation wave phase a path accumulates, expressed as the distance that would accumulate the same wave phase in vacuum. A centimetre in a uniform medium with refractive index 3/2 has optical path length 1.5cm, although its geometric length remains 1cm. This makes optical path length useful whenever two contributions must arrive with matching wave phases, from an optical lens to a Michelson interferometer. [ref]
For a specified path γ at fixed angular frequency ω, the optical path length is the line integral
OPLγ​(ω)=∫γ​n(r,ω)ds,ds=∣dr∣,OPL=∑j​nj​Lj​ for uniform segments.
(23)
Here s is geometric arc length, and n is the phase refractive index, evaluated at the same frequency everywhere. The propagation interpretation assumes a stationary linear medium with isotropy, a real positive scalar refractive index and negligible loss, on a valid geometrical optics branch. The path can curve; at sharp interfaces apply the appropriate matching conditions to each segment. A prescribed curve has a mathematical line integral, but it predicts a propagation wave phase only when it represents the physical branch. [ref] Optical fibers can require a mode wavenumber rather than the bulk refractive index along a guessed light ray. [ref]
Fix the vacuum wavelength λ0​=c/f=2πc/ω, with frequency f=ω/(2π) and vacuum wavenumber k0​=2π/λ0​. In a locally uniform medium the wavelength is λ=λ0​/n, while the frequency stays unchanged at a stationary interface. With the convention Φ=k0​S−ωt+ϕ0​, propagation from a specified starting wave phase contributes
ϕprop​=k0​OPL,δ=δref​+k0​(OPL2​−OPL1​)(mod2π).
(24)
The relative reference δref​ includes launch wave phases and any extra wave phase from mirrors, beam splitters or coatings. Thus k0​OPL is a propagation contribution, not an absolute detector wave phase independent of the apparatus. If the reference contributions stay fixed, a change in optical path difference h changes the phase difference by 2πh/λ0​. Using the material wavelength again in this formula would count the refractive index twice. [ref]
A motivating measurement turns invisible optical oscillations into a slowly changing electrical signal. MIT's teaching experiment uses a laser, a beam splitter, two returning mirrors, an amplified photodiode, an oscilloscope and a calibrated mirror actuator driven by a function generator. The returning beams overlap on the photodiode; one channel records detector voltage and another the actuator drive. The measured observable is the changing light intensity, including its maxima and minima, rather than direct timing of an optical cycle. A calibrated displacement per drive voltage and the spacing of the extrema relate geometric motion to the phase difference. The guide infers the laser wavelength from known actuator calibration; conversely, with independently known vacuum wavelength and ambient refractive index, the same relation calibrates mirror motion. These two unknowns cannot both be inferred from fringe spacing alone. [ref]
For a proposed change-of-medium measurement, keep the mirrors fixed and put a transparent cell of internal length L in one arm. Compare its contents at refractive indices na​ and nb​, leaving its windows in place. At normal incidence the two traversals give
ΔOPL=2L(nb​−na​),Δδ=λ0​4πL(nb​−na​)​,N=2πΔδ​=λ0​2L(nb​−na​)​.
(25)
Here N is the signed number of whole interference fringe cycles plus any resolved fractional cycle, counted continuously. A mirror displacement x instead gives ΔOPL=2namb​x; distinguish this double-pass factor from a single pass in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. OpenStax's gas-cell worked example provides the same double-pass reasoning; it is a teaching calculation rather than a published measurement dataset.[ref]
An exact toy calculation makes the sensitivity visible. Stipulate λ0​=600nm, L=10mm and nb​−na​=3/100000=0.00003. Then ΔOPL=600nm and Δδ=2π: a full interference fringe cycle, despite unchanged geometric lengths. For a continuous change nb​−na​=q(3/100000), let 0≤q≤2 and choose the initial detector phase difference to be zero. Equal coherent detected arm contributions of light intensity I0​ predict
4I0​I(q)​=21+cos(2πq)​=cos2(πq).
(26)
The plot is this stipulated model: q=1/2 gives a minimum, q=1 restores a maximum, and the reference level is chosen by adjustment of the apparatus. It contains no measured values or assigned properties of a real gas. The equivalent mirror travel in vacuum is 300nm per cycle. A single endpoint light intensity cannot distinguish q=0 from q=1; the continuous fringe count carries the missing information.
For an interpretable cell measurement, establish the initial phase difference with a small calibrated mirror scan, then track slow changes through successive interference fringes. Measure the dark signal and each arm separately, keep photodiode gain within its linear range, align both beams on the same region and match their linear polarizations. Monitor interferometric visibility and keep arm delays within the useful optical coherence time. Record cell length, contents, pressure and temperature; return to the starting condition to check drift. Changes in window deformation, cell length, external air or mirror position also change optical path length, so a reference cell or an independently monitored mechanical path is needed to isolate the contents' refractive index. These controls are deductions from the model, not a claim that the illustrated apparatus was operated. Loss of fringe count leaves a whole-cycle ambiguity; at an intensity extremum the first derivative with respect to phase difference vanishes, so a scan around phase quadrature is more sensitive to small changes. Broadband illumination, unstable optical coherence, vibration and strong loss can invalidate a simple one-frequency inference.

Group refractive index (ng​=n+ω∂ω​n)

The group refractive index is ng​=c/vg​ for a transparent isotropic propagation branch with forward group velocity vg​=dω/dk>0. Differentiating the local wavenumber k=n(ω)ω/c gives
ng​=n+ω∂ω∂n​=n−λ0​∂λ0​∂n​,τg​=∂ω∂ϕprop​​=c1​∫γ​ng​(r,ω)ds.
(27)
The last formula gives the propagation group delay along a path whose geometry is fixed as frequency varies; additional apparatus wave phases require their own frequency derivatives. For a narrow wave packet with little loss and negligible reshaping, it approximates the transit of its wave envelope. In the nondispersive case ∂ω​n=0, it reduces to OPL/c. An optical path length at one frequency contains no information about ∂ω​n, so in a medium with optical dispersion it cannot by itself determine the group delay. [ref]
For an original local model near ω∗​, choose two equal geometric paths of length L, with nA​(ω)=3/2 and nB​(ω)=3/2+(ω−ω∗​)/(10ω∗​). At ω∗​ both optical path lengths equal 3L/2, and matched launch and interface references give equal carrier wave phases. But ng,A​=3/2 and ng,B​=8/5, so their group delays differ by L/(10c). This local stipulated model is a counterexample to identifying equal wave phase with equal pulse arrival; it asserts no material response outside the narrow band considered. Strong loss or pulse reshaping requires a fuller propagation model, and group delay need not time the earliest causal response.

Interference (wave propagation)

Words: 3k Articles: 43
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Wave interference is the reinforcement or cancellation that occurs when overlapping wave amplitudes add by the superposition principle. For two monochromatic waves of the same frequency, mutual optical coherence means that their relative wave phase is stable during the observation. Equal wave phases give constructive interference; a half-cycle phase difference gives the destructive interference intensity minimum. Wave amplitudes add before their squares determine wave intensity. [ref].
Consider two overlapping beams in a homogeneous medium, with the same polarization of an electromagnetic wave and individual local time-averaged light intensities I1​,I2​. Their phase difference δ is measured in radians. In the scalar detection convention, the combined local time-averaged wave intensity is
I=I1​+I2​+2I1​I2​​cosδ.
(29)
The last term records wave interference; adding I1​+I2​ alone misses it. The formula describes irradiance when both fields propagate along the same direction, or when the same detector geometry factor is included in all three intensities. For crossing beams it describes the squared electric field response, proportional to scalar wave intensity; a specified component of the Poynting vector also requires the propagation geometry. The ideal crossing plane waves below make that distinction explicit.
For equal individual light intensities I1​=I2​=I0​>0, the cosine half-angle identity gives
I=2I0​(1+cosδ)=4I0​cos2(δ/2).
(30)
The constructive interference intensity is 4I0​ at δ=0 modulo 2π, and the destructive interference intensity is zero at δ=π modulo 2π. At phase quadrature, δ=π/2, it is 2I0​. With I1​=1 and I2​=0.25 in the same arbitrary wave intensity unit, the maximum is 2.25, the minimum is 0.25, and the phase quadrature value is 1.25: unequal wave amplitudes cannot cancel completely.
Both curves use the same wave intensity unit and a horizontal angle in radians. The dashed levels are the averages over a full phase difference cycle. Equal beams have interferometric visibility one; the unequal example has interferometric visibility 0.8.
A spatially varying phase difference turns the same law into interference fringes. Take two ideal plane electromagnetic waves with common wavelength λ, equal individual light intensities I0​, and propagation directions at angles +θ and −θ from the z axis in the xz plane, with 0<θ<π/2. Both have linear polarization along y, perpendicular to both propagation directions. Choose equal initial wave phases; their wavevectors and phase difference are
k±​=k(±sinθ,0,cosθ),k=λ2π​,ϕ±​=±kxsinθ+kzcosθ−ωt,δ=ϕ+​−ϕ−​=2kxsinθ.
(31)
Here k is the wavenumber and ω the angular frequency. The common z and time terms cancel, so the interference fringes stay at fixed x for every z. Their interference fringe spacing is
Λ=2ksinθ2π​=2sinθλ​,I0​I(x,z)​=4cos2(kxsinθ).
(32)
Set the length unit to λ, so that λ=1, and take θ=30∘=π/6: then Λ=1. The constructive interference intensity bands lie at integer x/λ; the destructive interference intensity bands lie at half-integer x/λ.
The grid covers −3≤x/λ≤3 and 0≤z/λ≤4; both axes are dimensionless lengths in wavelength units. The colour scale is I/I0​ from zero to four, using the same single-beam normalization as the equal-beam curve above. This is an ideal plane wave superposition, with no slits or point sources and no near-field approximation. For these y-polarized plane electromagnetic waves in vacuum, the longitudinal time-averaged Poynting vector obeys ⟨Sz​⟩=Icosθ; the plotted scalar I therefore differs from the irradiance through a plane normal to z by that common factor. This relation follows by adding the magnetic fields as well as the electric fields.
The bright peaks do not create energy. Averaging over one interference fringe spacing, or equivalently over one full phase difference cycle, gives
2π1​∫02π​I(δ)dδ=I1​+I2​,
(33)
because the integral of the cosine is zero, with sine as its antiderivative. Equal beams thus average to 2I0​, despite bright bands at 4I0​. For the crossing-wave geometry, the average longitudinal energy flux is correspondingly 2I0​cosθ. Bright and dark regions redistribute the incoming energy; conservation of energy concerns the full energy flux, rather than the height of one peak.
Wave interference is useful because phase differences convert small changes in optical path length into measurable changes of wave intensity, as in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Its beauty is that the same superposition principle produces both complete cancellation and fourfold brightening; adding more coherent contributions also produces the narrow peaks of a diffraction grating. Feynman's treatment connects this many-source pattern directly to addition of complex amplitudes. [ref].
A short proof outline uses local real fields Ej​(t)=Aj​cos(ωt+ϕj​) with parallel linear polarizations. Write I=C⟨(E1​+E2​)2⟩t​ and Ij​=CAj2​/2 for the same positive conversion factor C. Averaging over many wave periods while the phase difference stays fixed uses ⟨cos2(ωt+ϕj​)⟩t​=1/2 and ⟨cos(ωt+ϕ1​)cos(ωt+ϕ2​)⟩t​=cosδ/2, giving the stated law. Equivalently, add the complex amplitudes and take the squared complex modulus. [ref].
For different fixed linear polarizations in a common transverse plane, the cross term acquires the dot product of their real unit vectors, equal to cosα for relative angle α. Orthogonal linear polarizations remove the cross term in polarization-insensitive scalar detection; different orientations generally only reduce it. A common polarizer can select overlapping components and recover wave interference. Likewise, rapid random variation of the phase difference removes the observed cross term only when the detector's time average has ⟨eiδ(t)⟩t​=0. Slowly varying wave phases can instead move resolved interference fringes, and biased or incompletely sampled wave phases can leave residual contrast. Finite optical coherence therefore depends on the observation time as well as the fields.

Optical coherence

Words: 4k Articles: 24
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Optical coherence describes correlations between the wave amplitudes and wave phases of light sampled at different places or times. Its most direct classical test is wave interference: combine two samples of a field and see how much the detected light intensity changes when their relative wave phase is scanned. First-order optical coherence makes this statement quantitative; temporal optical coherence compares delayed samples, while spatial optical coherence compares different positions. These properties are relative to the samples and averaging procedure, rather than a single yes-or-no label for a source. [ref].
A useful surprise is that two copies of a fluctuating source can interfere strongly when they have matched delays: the copies share the fluctuations. Conversely, two individually steady-looking beams need not have correlated wave phases. The ideal diffraction grating calculation requires spatial optical coherence across its illuminated elements; unequal-arm measurements with a Michelson interferometer test temporal optical coherence.

Angular source size and spectral filtering control different correlations. Atmospheric phase fluctuations and instrument averaging can further reduce measured fringe visibility.

Michelson interferometer

A Michelson interferometer divides light at a beam splitter, reflects the two arms at mirrors and recombines the returning fields. For vacuum arm lengths ℓ1​,ℓ2​, the delay magnitude is ∣τ∣=2∣ℓ2​−ℓ1​∣/c. At each coarse delay, a small mirror scan produces maxima and minima of the detected light intensity. A photodiode and its electrical readout resolve these changes; the scan should cover several carrier cycles while changing ∣g(1)∣ negligibly. MIT's laboratory guide uses a mirror actuator, photodiode and electrical drive to scan interference fringes and extract interferometric visibility.[ref]
A verified motivating experiment is Shaoul Ezekiel's MIT demonstration of source-spectrum control. A polarizer selects one or several lines from a laser whose adjacent lines have orthogonal linear polarizations. A sampled beam goes to a scanning Fabry–Pérot interferometer to check the optical spectrum; the main beam enters a Michelson interferometer, and a lens projects its interference fringes onto a screen. With one selected line the fringes retain good contrast through the demonstrated delay range. With several lines their contrast falls and returns as the arm length changes. At a fixed delay with poor contrast, selecting one line restores it; at matched arms both selections give good contrast. This control isolates the role of spectral composition rather than simply the arm position. The presentation is a qualitative demonstration, not a calibrated linewidth measurement. [ref].
A deliberately simpler two-line model explains the return of contrast. Take two stationary, mutually uncorrelated monochromatic contributions of equal power at ν0​±δν/2. Their normalized wave-field correlation is
g(1)(τ)=e−i2πν0​τcos(πδντ),V(τ)=∣cos(πδντ)∣
(54)
for equal detected single-arm light intensities. At τ=1/(2δν) the two contributions' interference fringes cancel on averaging; at τ=1/δν they agree again. This is a deduction from the stipulated spectrum, not a fit to Ezekiel's two- or three-line source. Finite individual linewidths eventually damp these revivals.
For a quantitative version of the experiment, the visibility law suggests explicit controls. Measure each arm separately at every coarse delay, subtract the detector's dark signal and any measured background, then normalize by 2I1​I2​​/(I1​+I2​). Keep the returning beams aligned on the same detector region with parallel linear polarizations; keep detector gain fixed and avoid saturation. Resolve the small mirror scan electrically, rather than averaging over its moving interference fringes. Repeat scans to identify vibration or drift. These controls follow from the averaging and mode-matching assumptions in first-order optical coherence; loss of contrast alone cannot distinguish source decorrelation from apparatus motion, misalignment or insufficient spatial resolution. The finite travel range gives access only to a finite range of delays.
The practical gain is that wave interference measures field correlations even when the detector cannot follow the optical oscillation itself. A long optical coherence length allows unequal-arm measurements; a short one localizes high contrast near matched delays. The beautiful feature is that both fading and reappearance of interference fringes are sums of the same rotating complex amplitudes.

A Michelson interferometer turns displacement into a count of interference fringes: a moving mirror changes both the outward and return paths. This lets a wavelength act as a ruler whose divisions need no engraving. Assume normal incidence, a fixed reference arm, stable refractive index n along the moving arm, and fixed vacuum wavelength λ0​. Write λ=λ0​/n for the wavelength in that medium and take ΔL positive away from the beam splitter. The change in optical path difference, the accumulated phase difference, and the signed number of complete interference fringe cycles are
ΔD=2nΔL,Δϕ=λ0​2πΔD​=λ4πΔL​,ΔN=2πΔϕ​=λ2ΔL​,ΔL=2λΔN​.
(55)
The factor two comes from propagation geometry: moving the mirror by ΔL adds ΔL before reflection and ΔL afterward. One bright-to-bright cycle means mirror travel λ/2; bright-to-dark means λ/4, half a cycle. All lengths must use compatible units, and ΔN is dimensionless. A constant reflection phase difference changes the initial fringe position but cancels from this change formula.
For an original hypothetical example, suppose λ=600nm in the actual surrounding medium and a continuous scan gives 40.25 cycles, including the final fractional cycle. Then ΔL=(600nm)(40.25)/2=12075nm=12.075μm. With the wavelength treated as exact, a fringe-reading measurement uncertainty of 0.02 cycle contributes 6nm to the displacement measurement uncertainty. An uncertainty of 0.01rad in a local phase difference instead corresponds to 600(0.01)/(4π)nm≈0.477nm. This illustrates measurement resolution, not a complete claim of accuracy: wavelength calibration, air changes, mirror tilt and missed cycles can dominate.
To separate the oscillating readout from its optical coherence envelope, use the local model
I(D)=Iˉ[1+V(D)cos(λ0​2πD​+ϕb​)],D=2(n2​L2​−n1​L1​).

Here I is detected light intensity, Iˉ is the mean level, ϕb​ is a fixed bias wave phase, and V is interferometric visibility. A fine scan of D measures the carrier phase difference; a coarse scan can map the temporal optical coherence envelope through V(D). The envelope maximum locates matched delays only under the source and apparatus assumptions; it is not a bright fringe identifying an arbitrary mirror position. Even with known V, one intensity reading leaves the cosine sign and whole-cycle ambiguities. Continuous motion of known direction, or an independently obtained pair of signals in phase quadrature, is needed to recover signed travel through reversals.
The figure's original control example stipulates equal arm light intensities, matching linear polarizations, and a Lorentzian optical spectrum giving V(D)=exp(−∣D∣/Lc​) with Lc​=1mm. In vacuum, arm mismatches ∣L2​−L1​∣=0.60mm and 0.10mm give V=e−1.2≈0.301 and e−0.2≈0.819. Matching the arms improves the phase difference readout without changing its λ0​/2 travel per cycle. A fine mirror scan of one cycle changes D by only 600nm for the stipulated 600nm source, much less than Lc​. These are calculated values, not historical data.
A proposed measurement sequence follows from this model. Overlap the returning beams, match their linear polarizations, find a high-contrast delay and use a small calibrated mirror scan to determine the sign and fringe period. Read a fixed spatial sample of the interference fringes with a photodiode; record each arm separately and the dark signal, avoid detector saturation, and retain enough time resolution to count every cycle. Approach mechanical settings consistently and repeat the return scan to expose lost motion or drift. For very small changes, bias near phase quadrature, where ∣dI/dϕ∣=IˉV is largest; an intensity extremum has zero first-order sensitivity. A known drive voltage alone does not provide measurement calibration for mirror travel: compare the actual travel with the fringe count using an independently known wavelength.
Control temperature, pressure, vibration and air currents because the instrument measures optical path difference, not mirror motion alone. For a fixed reference arm and fixed λ0​, the first-order change of the moving arm's round-trip path is ΔD≈2nΔL+2LΔn. Thus an unrecognized Δn mimics ΔLapp​=LΔn/n. A hypothetical L=0.10m, n≈1, and Δn=10−7 give 10nm apparent travel. Holding the mirror still while varying or monitoring the air conditions tests this confounder. Separate checks of alignment, wavelength stability and thermal expansion are necessary before sub-fringe measurement resolution becomes a defensible measurement uncertainty.
Michelson measurement of length in cadmium wavelengths
Words: 253
Michelson interferometer OurBigBook.com
Albert Abraham Michelson's 1907 lecture, Recent Advances in Spectroscopy, pp. 171–172, connects counting interference fringes with a reproducible length standard. Broad or multiple spectral lines obscured fringes at large path differences; red cadmium emission supplied a suitable source. His 1907 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized optical precision instruments and their spectroscopy and metrology applications.[ref]
His authored account of the metre comparison at Sèvres describes a heated, evacuated cadmium discharge tube and a spectrometer selecting one spectral line. A movable reference mirror was compared with pairs of silvered parallel surfaces defining intermediate standards. Counted interference fringes established a short interval; repeated comparisons extended it to a decimetre and then a metre. White-light fringes located surface coincidence, while monochromatic fringes supplied counts and fractional orders. A thermally shielding box, firm pier, calibrated translation screw and tested thermometers controlled drafts, vibration, travel and temperature. Uniform temperature mattered in comparisons; the final standard required an absolute temperature reading. Optical microscopes made the final comparison to the marked metre bar, limiting the whole result.[ref]
This is a measurement chain, rather than one enormous unchecked fringe count: short intervals establish whole orders; fractional-order readings refine each longer comparison. The optical coherence envelope helps locate white-light coincidence, whereas the carrier phase difference measures small departures from it. Repetition checks counting mistakes, but agreement alone cannot exclude shared systematic errors. The general lesson of metrology is to preserve the link from the optical ruler through each transfer and control to the final length.

Two small openings separated by d sample this correlation: recombine their light with nearly matched travel times and measure interferometric visibility near the central interference fringes. A narrow opening in front of a broad-spectrum lamp can improve transverse spatial optical coherence while leaving its short temporal optical coherence. MIT's lecture notes illustrate the two-opening test and these contrasting source preparations. [ref].
To isolate source width, stipulate a distant, narrowband source with uniform angular brightness on −Θ/2≤α≤Θ/2, and mutually uncorrelated emission from distinct source directions. Here Θ≪1 is the full angular width in radians, λ the common wavelength, and the two openings are separated by d along the same transverse direction as the source extent. Neglect amplitude differences across the openings. Each source direction contributes a phase difference approximately 2πdα/λ. Averaging its complex cross term gives

Increasing w overlays more mutually incoherent, displaced interference fringe patterns. Restrict the recorded region so the path difference stays small compared with the optical coherence length, and resolve the fringes with the detector. This protocol is a model-based extension of the verified two-opening method, not a claim that the plotted curves were measured.
Thus an extended incoherent source can give locally excellent wave interference when the sampled separation is small, and almost none when it is larger. Diffraction grating

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
A diffraction grating is a periodic optical structure whose repeated slits or grooves direct light into diffraction orders through wave interference. Its beauty is that many individually broad contributions cooperate to select narrow directions: the spacing determines where the principal peaks occur, while the number of illuminated elements determines how sharply they are selected. This makes a diffraction grating useful in a spectrometer, where separating wavelengths spatially lets us examine an optical spectrum. [ref].
Consider a transmission diffraction grating in air, illuminated at normal incidence by a plane wave. Let d be the centre-to-centre slit spacing, λ the wavelength in the surrounding medium, and θ the signed outgoing angle from the forward normal. In Fraunhofer diffraction, where observation directions specify the far-field pattern, adjacent contributions have path difference dsinθ and phase difference δ=2πdsinθ/λ. Their wave amplitudes reinforce whenever δ=2πm, giving dsinθ=mλ. This normal-incidence geometry should be kept distinct from the incident and reflected angle convention in the grating equation below. [ref].
Angular colour separation follows immediately. At fixed nonzero diffraction order, increasing the wavelength moves the peak farther from the normal. With d=2μm, first-order light at 450nm leaves at 13.003∘, whereas 650nm leaves at 18.966∘: a separation of 5.963∘. The zero diffraction order stays at 0∘ for both wavelengths. Thus grating dispersion comes from an orderly dependence of wave interference on wavelength, rather than an arbitrary assignment of colours to directions.
For N identical slits with uniform coherent illumination, meaning stable relative wave phases across the array, the normalized wave interference factor is
FN​(θ)=​N1​∑j=0N−1​eijδ​2=[Nsin(δ/2)sin(Nδ/2)​]2,δ=λ2πdsinθ​.
(58)
The apparent 0/0 at a principal peak has limiting value one. A short explanation uses the geometric series: equal wave phases add N equal complex amplitudes; a small directional change distributes those contributions around the complex plane and allows cancellation. With each slit's contribution held fixed, peak scalar wave intensity scales as N2. The normalized plots remove that height change to make the narrowing visible. Stable relative wave phases, or optical coherence, are essential; a sum of independent intensities would lose this array structure. [ref].
For finite slit width a, the ideal rectangular-slit model multiplies FN​ by a broad single-slit diffraction envelope:
I(0)I(θ)​=[usinu​]2FN​(θ),u=λπasinθ​.
(59)
The sinc function factor, extended continuously at u=0, controls the brightness available to the narrow peaks. For example, a=0.5μm gives envelope values about 0.811, 0.405, and 0.090 at diffraction orders 1, 2, and 3 in the 600nm example. If an envelope zero coincides with an allowed diffraction order, that peak disappears. A permitted direction therefore need not produce a visible bright spot. [ref].
Historically, Joseph von Fraunhofer used fine parallel wires stretched between threaded rods to make diffraction gratings. Kenyon's historical apparatus account describes both this construction and a later reconstruction with visible light. The example makes the governing idea tangible: regular spacing can turn a simple array of obstacles into an instrument for distinguishing wavelengths. [ref].

Anamorphic magnification of a grating OurBigBook.com
A slit of width x at the focus of a collimator subtends x/fcoll​. Its projected width is xfcam​cosα/(fcoll​cosβ). Dividing this width by the grating dispersion gives Δλ=xdcosα/(mfcoll​). Thus the spectral resolving power is R=mλfcoll​/(xdcosα). Omitting the anamorphic factor gives a denominator cosβ instead; these agree in the Littrow configuration.

Littrow configuration

Words: 19
Diffraction grating OurBigBook.com
In the Littrow configuration the selected diffracted ray retraces the incident ray, so α=β and the grating equation becomes mλ=2dsinα.

Echelle grating

Words: 16
Diffraction grating OurBigBook.com
An echelle grating works in high diffraction orders. A separate cross-disperser separates their overlapping optical spectra on a two-dimensional detector.

Free spectral range (ΔλFSR​)

Words: 184 Articles: 2
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
The free spectral range is the wavelength or frequency spacing between adjacent orders or resonances of an optical instrument. It identifies when different orders can overlap. Always specify the coordinate: a uniform spacing in frequency need not be uniform in wavelength. For an ideal Fabry–Pérot interferometer at normal incidence, with mirror separation d and constant refractive index n, Fabry–Pérot resonance spacing gives ΔνFSR​=c/(2nd), where c is the speed of light in vacuum. The free spectral range of an echelle grating follows a different order condition.

Free spectral range of an echelle grating

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Free spectral range OurBigBook.com
At fixed incident and central outgoing angles, the grating equation gives mλm​=K=d(sinα+sinβ0​). Adjacent central wavelengths are separated by
λm​−λm+1​=m(m+1)K​∼mλm​​.
(63)
This is the usual adjacent-order free spectral range. A detector width of approximately qΔλFSR​, where q is the grating dispersion, covers one such interval.

Adjacent-order spacing versus nearest-axis echelle interval (Scentres​=K/[m(m+1)])

Words: 79
Free spectral range of an echelle grating OurBigBook.com
At a fixed camera-axis direction, the grating equation gives mλm​=K=d(sinα+sinβ0​), so adjacent central wavelengths differ by K/[m(m+1)]. This differs from the exact wavelength cell where an order is nearest the optical camera axis. For β0​=0 and x=ftanβ, equal distances of orders m and m+1 mean opposite diffraction angles; adding their diffraction grating equations gives λ=K/(m+1/2). The full order-m cell is bounded by K/(m+1/2) and K/(m−1/2), hence has width K/(m2−1/4) for m≥2 and accessible neighbouring orders. Both widths approach K/m2 at high order.

Speckle pattern

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
A speckle pattern is a granular intensity pattern from coherent wave interference. In stellar imaging, residual wavefront errors produce speckles around the central point spread function.

Speckle contrast of a sinusoidal wavefront error (C=(πh0​/λ)2)

Words: 66
Speckle pattern OurBigBook.com
For a small sinusoidal optical path length error h0​cos(2πx/Λ), expand its phase factor to first order. The two exponential harmonics each have field amplitude iπh0​/λ relative to the unperturbed field, so each speckle has contrast C=(πh0​/λ)2. Its angular displacement is λ/Λ. Here h0​ is optical path error, not physical mirror displacement; a reflecting mirror introduces twice its surface displacement in the near-normal limit.

Amplitude transmittance (t=Uout​/Uin​)

Words: 46
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Amplitude transmittance is the local ratio of transmitted to incident complex amplitude in a thin optical-element model. It includes wave phase as well as attenuation. For identical incident and transmitted media at normal incidence, the corresponding intensity transmittance is ∣t∣2; t itself is not the transmitted power fraction. A pure phase screen has ∣t∣=1.

Holography

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Holography records the wave interference between a holographic object wave and a known holographic reference wave, then uses that record to reconstruct a wavefront. The record is a hologram. A photographic plate or photodetector measures light intensity; the relative wave phase is encoded in the positions and contrast of interference fringes, rather than measured directly as an optical oscillation. Reillumination makes the recorded pattern act as a diffraction grating that produces an image-bearing field.
The useful change of viewpoint is to preserve a field that can propagate again, instead of only a focused brightness picture. Recovered complex amplitude permits refocusing with the Fresnel propagator; a spatially extended hologram can also supply different viewing directions. The recoverable information is limited by the collected aperture, recorded spatial frequencies, optical coherence and separation of unwanted diffraction orders.

Electron holography

Words: 18
Holography OurBigBook.com
Electron holography uses electron object and reference waves to encode their relative wave phase in a hologram.[ref]

Hologram

Words: 40
Holography OurBigBook.com
A hologram is the recorded wave interference pattern used for holographic wavefront reconstruction. The pattern need not resemble the object. A photographic emulsion stores a material change produced by exposure; a digital intensity record instead requires numerical reconstruction or a device that displays the corresponding optical modulation.

Holographic reference wave (R)

Words: 40
Holography OurBigBook.com
A holographic reference wave is a known coherent comparison field at the recording surface. Its wave phase supplies the standard against which the holographic object wave is encoded. In in-line holography, the undiffracted part of the illumination can supply this field; in off-axis holography, a separate tilted beam supplies it.

Holographic object wave (O)

Words: 37
Holography OurBigBook.com
A holographic object wave is the object-dependent field arriving at the recording surface, including the propagation from the object. Its complex amplitude generally differs from the transmission function at the object itself. Distinguishing these two planes is essential when refocusing a hologram.

Holographic wavefront reconstruction (I=∣R+O∣2)

Words: 364
Holography OurBigBook.com
Take stationary scalar monochromatic waves of the same frequency and polarization of an electromagnetic wave, with time convention e−iωt. Write their complex amplitudes at the recording plane as R=AR​eiϕR​ and O=AO​eiϕO​, absorbing the common conversion to irradiance into the units. An exposure short enough to avoid fringe motion but long compared with an optical period records
I=∣R+O∣2=∣R∣2+∣O∣2+R∗O+RO∗=AR2​+AO2​+2AR​AO​cos(ϕO​−ϕR​).
(64)
The two cross terms are where relative wave phase enters the measured light intensity. Blocking the holographic reference wave leaves ∣O∣2 and removes them. Loss of mutual optical coherence, incompatible polarization of an electromagnetic wave or motion that averages the relative wave phase similarly reduces fringe contrast. These are useful controls for distinguishing a hologram from an ordinary brightness record. One local cosine value does not uniquely determine a wave phase; known reference structure and separation of the cross terms supply the additional information in the example below.
Model a thin weakly modulated recording by its amplitude transmittance
t=t0​+βI,∣βI∣≪∣t0​∣.
(65)
Here t0​ and β are real constants in a local linear response to exposure at a fixed exposure time. They describe a chosen amplitude modulation model, not a universal photographic response; an absorbing negative may have β<0. Keep 0≤t≤1 for this passive real-transmission model. Ignore material thickness, saturation, shrinking, clipping and changes of wavelength. Illuminating the processed record with the original R gives, immediately after the plate,
Rt=zero-order background[t0​+β(∣R∣2+∣O∣2)]R​​+desired object fieldβ∣R∣2O​​+conjugate fieldβR2O∗​​.
(66)
This follows by multiplying the preceding identity by R; no wave phase detector has been assumed. If ∣R∣ is uniform, the desired term reproduces O up to a constant. A nonuniform ∣R∣2 weights the recovered field. With a strong holographic reference wave, the ∣O∣2R contamination is small relative to ∣R∣2R, but it is retained in this identity. Subsequent diffraction propagates each term: reproduction at the plate is the starting boundary field, not yet a focused image.
The schematic uses a plane wave reference and one optical point source to separate the functions. The top row records R+O; the bottom removes the object and illuminates the developed hologram with R. Dashed extensions identify the desired virtual image; the conjugate component converges toward a real image. All three outgoing components coexist. The coloured paths distinguish terms, not different wavelengths; distances and strengths are schematic. This functional drawing is not a reconstruction of the historical apparatus.

In-line holography

Words: 254 Articles: 1
Holography OurBigBook.com
In-line holography uses nearly the same direction for the holographic reference wave and holographic object wave. In a transmission geometry, the undiffracted illumination supplies R while the object supplies the scattered component O. This makes small optical path differences possible, but leaves the desired image, its twin image in holography and the bright background sharing an axis.
Dennis Gabor's electron-microscopy motivation led to optical tests: one line of a high-pressure mercury-vapor lamp illuminated a 3 μm pinhole, then approximately 1 mm microphotographs, recording approximately 1 cm holograms on sensitive photographic emulsions with minute-scale exposures. The roughly 0.1 mm optical coherence length favoured an in-line arrangement. Reillumination reconstructed images; focusing separated their depths incompletely. Distorted letters and random optical disturbances limited the results. These were optical demonstrations, not an operating electron microscope.[ref]
The recorded microphotograph and its reconstructed lettering provide an object-to-image comparison in that account. The blocked-reference control described above is an explanatory control for the model; it is not a claim about an additional historical measurement.

Twin image in holography

Words: 96
In-line holography OurBigBook.com
For a uniform on-axis plane wave reference, choose its constant wave phase to be zero, so R=AR​>0. The reconstructed cross terms are then proportional to O and its complex conjugate O∗. This pair creates the twin image in holography. An outgoing curved wavefront and its conjugate have opposite curvature: under forward propagation, one can appear to diverge from a virtual image while the other converges to a real image. In in-line holography their depths differ, but a defocused member still overlaps the other. This is the same conjugation of spatial wave phase used in phase conjugation, although a transmission hologram here launches both components forward rather than automatically creating a returning phase-conjugate mirror.

Off-axis holography

Words: 399
Holography OurBigBook.com
Off-axis holography tilts the holographic reference wave relative to the holographic object wave. Its interference fringes acquire a carrier spatial frequency; the two cross terms occupy different spatial frequency regions when the carrier is sufficiently large compared with the object's signal bandwidth. This permits filtering a single image term.
Gabor's lecture credits Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks with the later skew-reference method using helium–neon laser illumination, separating reconstructed images angularly.[ref]
For an original periodic calculation, let x run over a unit-length interval and choose
O(x)=0.2e2πi3x+0.1e−2πi5x,R(x)=e2πi20x.
(67)
All spatial frequencies here are cycles per unit length; the data are a chosen field at the recording plane, not measurements or a physical object profile. Direct expansion gives
I(x)=1.05+0.04cos(2π8x)+0.4cos(2π17x)+0.2cos(2π25x).
(68)
Consequently its Fourier series coefficients are 1.05 at zero, 0.02 at ±8, 0.2 at ±17 and 0.1 at ±25. The R∗O component lies at −17,−25; the RO∗ component lies at 17,25; the background lies at 0,±8. Filtering the negative-frequency cross term and multiplying by R recovers O, including its relative wave phase.
The figure samples N=1024 equally spaced positions with the endpoint excluded, computes a normalized discrete Fourier transform using a Fast Fourier transform, retains bins −30≤m≤−12, then applies the inverse discrete Fourier transform and multiplies by R. The recovered real and imaginary parts coincide with the chosen O to numerical precision. This exact periodic example avoids leakage by placing every frequency on an integer bin; finite nonperiodic records need allowance for broadening and an aperture.
For a continuous object field with Fourier transform confined to ∣f∣≤B, the background ∣O∣2 occupies ∣f∣≤2B. A carrier fc​>3B is a sufficient separation condition for the sideband centred at −fc​, and fc​+B must remain below the Nyquist spatial frequency. Here B=5, fc​=20 and the Nyquist spatial frequency is 512. This sufficient bound describes a whole bandwidth, rather than exploiting the gaps in this particular two-component field.
The same example also makes optical playback explicit. Choose t0​=0.3 and β=0.01. Since ∣O∣≤0.3, the bounds 0.49≤I≤1.69 imply 0.3049≤t≤0.3169, and ∣βI∣/t0​≤0.0564. The affine response is stipulated; its weak-modulation interpretation is approximate. In Rt, the desired field 0.01O has frequencies 3,−5; the conjugate term 0.01R2O∗ has frequencies 37,45; the background has frequencies 20,12,28. Thus the same carrier that separates the recorded cross terms separates the playback components. Reillumination restores a field through diffraction; computational filtering extracts the corresponding encoded field through Fourier analysis.
